lessons.title: Lazy arguments and force
lessons.summary: Insert force(x) as the first statement of choose. What happens for the same call?
explanation: A supplied function argument is usually a promise: its expression and calling environment are retained until the value is needed. An unused argument can therefore contain an expression that would fail if evaluated. stop(message) raises an error and interrupts normal execution.
force(x) evaluates the promise for x now. It is useful before returning a closure that should retain the current argument value. It does not recursively force every promise stored elsewhere.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
choose <- function(x, use) {
  if (use) x else 7
}
cat(choose(stop("evaluated"), FALSE), "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Replace stop with a visible message and compare the timing with and without force. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Dot-dot-dot and argument matching
lessons.summary: Replace remove = TRUE with rem = 1. What prints?
explanation: ... collects arguments not matched to other formal parameters and can forward them into another call. sum(..., na.rm = remove) passes those values to sum and separately sets its missing-value policy.

Formal parameters after ... must be matched by their exact names. Partial names are not matched to remove here. sum adds numeric values; without na.rm = TRUE, a missing value makes this result missing. A numeric argument accidentally captured by ... becomes data, not an option.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
total <- function(..., remove = FALSE) {
  sum(..., na.rm = remove)
}
cat(total(1, NA, remove = TRUE), "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Closures and retained environments
lessons.summary: Remove force(amount), keeping the later base <- 9. What prints?
explanation: A closure combines a function with the environment where it was defined. The returned function can still find amount in the completed make_adder call’s environment.

force(amount) evaluates the supplied base expression while base is 2. Without forcing before return, the retained promise can evaluate that expression later, after the caller changes base. A closure retains bindings and environments, not automatically frozen snapshots of all names.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
make_adder <- function(amount) {
  force(amount)
  function(x) x + amount
}
base <- 2
add <- make_adder(base)
base <- 9
cat(add(3), "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 5. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Environments and reference semantics
lessons.summary: Replace new.env(parent = emptyenv()) with list(). What prints?
explanation: new.env creates an environment, a mutable mapping from names to values. Assigning it to alias does not copy the environment; both names refer to the same bindings. $ reads or assigns a named binding in this example.

parent = emptyenv() makes this a data-only environment with no inherited bindings. Ordinary lists use value-like copy-on-modify behavior, while environments are intentionally shared. Do not infer that changing any R object through an alias always updates the original.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
state <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
state$count <- 1
alias <- state
alias$count <- 4
cat(state$count, "\n")
```

lessons.title: Attributes and class meaning
lessons.summary: Change the unit attribute to hours. Does the numeric storage convert?
explanation: attr(x, name) reads a named attribute; assigning through it attaches metadata. Attributes can record names, dimensions, class or a custom unit. This custom unit label does not itself convert numbers or enforce a unit system.

typeof reports the underlying R type. class reports the class used by many higher-level operations; setting a class label does not validate that the object satisfies its intended contract. Special attributes can alter interpretation without replacing the stored numbers.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(10, 20)
attr(values, "unit") <- "minutes"
cat(attr(values, "unit"), "\n")
cat(typeof(values), "\n")
```

double. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: S3 generics and method dispatch
lessons.summary: Change class = "minutes" to class = "other". What prints?
explanation: UseMethod("describe") selects a method according to the class of the generic’s first argument. describe.minutes names a method for the minutes class; describe.default is the fallback when no matching class method is found.

structure(5, class = "minutes") creates the value with a class attribute. This S3 tag is informal: production constructors must check their own invariants. Call the generic rather than guessing a method name at each call site.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
describe <- function(x) UseMethod("describe")
describe.minutes <- function(x) "timed"
describe.default <- function(x) "ordinary"
x <- structure(5, class = "minutes")
cat(describe(x), "\n")
```

lessons.title: Errors and tryCatch

lessons.title: Warnings and calling handlers
lessons.summary: Replace withCallingHandlers with tryCatch, and replace invokeRestart("muffleWarning") with 9. What prints?
explanation: warning signals a condition but normally allows evaluation to continue. withCallingHandlers runs a matching handler in the signaling context. This differs from tryCatch’s exiting handler, which abandons that expression’s remaining normal path.

invokeRestart("muffleWarning") invokes the restart provided by warning to suppress its default reporting after the handler has recorded it. This is not blanket suppression of all failures. The returned result still comes from the code after warning.

lessons.title: Cleanup with on.exit
lessons.summary: Change work() to work(TRUE). What prints after the error is caught?
explanation: on.exit records an expression to run when the current function exits normally or through an error. Register cleanup as soon as a resource or temporary state needs restoring. add = TRUE adds a cleanup expression instead of replacing an earlier one.

The on.exit expression here restores a shared environment binding; it does not replace the normal return value. Cleanup can itself fail, so keep it reliable and avoid masking the original failure. This example changes only a local fixture environment, not global configuration.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
state <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
state$active <- FALSE
work <- function(fail = FALSE) {
  state$active <- TRUE
  on.exit(state$active <- FALSE, add = TRUE)
  if (fail) stop("failed")
  5
}
result <- tryCatch(work(), error = function(e) -1)
cat(result, state$active, "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 5 FALSE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: List apply and type-stable vapply
lessons.summary: Replace sum with function(x) x, keeping numeric(1). What happens?
explanation: lapply returns one list element per input element, preserving a list result even when values are simple. vapply additionally requires each function result to match an explicit length and compatible type template.

numeric(1) is a length-one double template here. Each sum returns one numeric total. vapply may promote compatible simpler types, but it rejects an incompatible result length or type rather than silently choosing a different output shape as sapply can.

```r
values <- list(c(1, 2), c(4, 5))
result <- vapply(values, sum, numeric(1))
```

lessons.title: Ordering and duplicated keys
lessons.summary: Remove scores from order(keys, scores). What changes in the first line?
explanation: order(keys, scores) returns row positions sorted by keys, breaking equal-key ties with scores. For this default ordering, unresolved ties retain their original relative order. Apply the same index to every aligned column; sorting one column alone breaks row relationships.

duplicated marks occurrences after the first equal value. It does not automatically merge or remove all rows belonging to repeated keys. To detect a nonunique key policy, use those flags deliberately rather than assuming sorting removes duplicates.

```r
scores <- c(1, 3, 2)
i <- order(keys, scores)

cat(duplicated(keys), "\n")
```

lessons.title: Merging tables and key multiplicity
lessons.summary: Replace the right table with one row id = 1, label = "a". How many joined rows remain?
explanation: merge(left, right, by = "id") combines rows with equal id values. Its default is an inner join: unmatched keys are omitted. all.x = TRUE retains unmatched left rows with missing right-side values.

Repeated keys can create multiple row pairs: two matching left rows and two matching right rows produce four joined rows. Validate key uniqueness when your model expects one-to-one or many-to-one relationships. Do not silently interpret duplicated joins as new independent observations.

lessons.title: Reshaping repeated measurements
lessons.summary: Change the day labels times = c(1, 2) to times = c(10, 20). What changes in the printed row count and sum?
explanation: A wide table stores day1 and day2 in separate columns. A long table stores a day identifier and one minutes column, with repeated id values. This changes the layout, not the underlying measurements.

reshape uses varying for the measurement columns, v.names for their shared value name, timevar and times for the new occasion labels, and idvar for the entity identifier. direction = "long" selects this conversion. Verify unique entity/occasion pairs before trying a reverse wide transformation.

```r
                timevar = "day", times = c(1, 2), idvar = "id", direction = "long")

cat(sum(long$minutes), "\n")
```

lessons.title: The native pipe and explicit calls
lessons.summary: Change na.rm = TRUE to na.rm = FALSE. What prints?
explanation: The native |> pipe normally inserts its left expression as the first argument of the call on the right. This expression is equivalent to sum(c(1, NA, 3), na.rm = TRUE); it is ordinary R syntax, not a package dependency.

To place the value explicitly in a named argument, a named _ placeholder can be used once in an eligible call, such as value |> round(x = _, digits = 1). A pipe does not automatically vectorize a scalar-only function or change its missing-value behavior.

lessons.title: Regular expressions and replacements
lessons.summary: Remove fixed = TRUE from both calls. What prints?
explanation: grepl returns one logical match result per input string. With fixed = TRUE the dot is literal; without it, dot is a regular-expression wildcard matching a character. Know which interpretation your input needs.

gsub replaces every match and returns strings; sub replaces only the first match in each string. Neither evaluates the replacement as R code. Complex regular expressions and unbounded external input need separate performance and validation limits.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:

```r
cat(grepl(".", text, fixed = TRUE), "\n")
cat(gsub(".", "-", text, fixed = TRUE), "\n")
```

lessons.title: Dates time zones and instants
lessons.summary: Change instant + 3600 to instant + 1. What time prints on the second line?
explanation: as.Date represents calendar dates, and adding a number adds days. as.POSIXct represents instants; adding a number adds seconds. Specify a time zone when parsing clock text to avoid relying on the session’s local zone.

format turns values into display strings. %Y-%m-%d selects a date and %H:%M selects hours and minutes. Regional daylight-saving rules mean one calendar day is not always 86400 elapsed seconds; the fixture uses UTC deliberately and does not assert regional behavior.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
date <- as.Date("2025-01-01")
cat(format(date + 1, "%Y-%m-%d"), "\n")
instant <- as.POSIXct("2025-01-01 00:30:00", tz = "UTC")
cat(format(instant + 3600, tz = "UTC", format = "%H:%M"), "\n")
```

01:30. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Namespaces libraries and package boundaries
lessons.summary: Replace stats::median with median in the last line. What prints?
explanation: library attaches an installed package’s exported names to the search path. Another binding can mask an unqualified name. package::name selects that package’s exported object directly without attaching all of its names; it does not install a missing package.

stats is included in this R installation. Its median selects the middle ordered value for this odd-length vector. A local function named median can coexist with stats::median. Avoid package:::internal as an application contract: unexported internals may change. Record R and package versions; do not assume an attached package implies the latest release.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
median <- function(x) -1
cat(median(c(1, 9, 5)), "\n")
cat(stats::median(c(1, 9, 5)), "\n")
```
